{{Short description|Classifications of Lorentzian manifolds}}
'''Causality conditions''' are classifications of [[Lorentzian manifold]]s according to the types of [[causal structure]]s they admit.
In the study of [[spacetime]]s, there exists a hierarchy of causality conditions which are important in proving mathematical theorems about the global structure of such manifolds. 
These conditions were collected during the late 1970s.<ref name="CausalLadder">E. Minguzzi and M. Sanchez, ''The causal hierarchy of spacetimes'' in [[Helga Baum|H. Baum]] and D. Alekseevsky (eds.), vol. Recent developments in pseudo-Riemannian geometry, ESI Lect. Math. Phys., (Eur. Math. Soc. Publ. House, Zurich, 2008), pp. 299–358, {{ISBN|978-3-03719-051-7}}, [[arXiv:gr-qc/0609119]]</ref>

The weaker the causality condition on a spacetime, the more ''unphysical'' the spacetime is. Spacetimes with [[closed timelike curve]]s, for example, present severe interpretational difficulties. See the [[grandfather paradox]].

It is reasonable to believe that any physical spacetime will satisfy the strongest causality condition: [[global hyperbolicity]]. For such spacetimes the equations in [[general relativity]] can be posed as an [[initial value problem]] on a [[Cauchy surface]].

== The hierarchy ==

There is a hierarchy of causality conditions, each one of which is strictly stronger than the previous. This is sometimes called the '''causal ladder'''. The conditions, from weakest to strongest, are:

* Non-totally vicious
* Chronological
* Causal
* Distinguishing
* Strongly causal
* Stably causal
* Causally continuous
* Causally simple
* [[Globally hyperbolic]]

Given are the definitions of these causality conditions for a Lorentzian manifold <math>(M,g)</math>. Where two or more are given they are equivalent.

'''Notation''':
* <math>p \ll q</math> denotes the [[chronological relation]].
* <math>p \prec q</math> denotes the [[causal relation]].
(See [[Causal structure#Causal relations|causal structure]] for definitions of <math>\,I^+(x)</math>, <math>\,I^-(x)</math> and  <math>\,J^+(x)</math>, <math>\,J^-(x)</math>.)

== Non-totally vicious ==

* For some points <math>p \in M</math> we have <math>p \not\ll p</math>.

== Chronological ==

* There are no closed chronological (timelike) curves.
* The [[chronological relation]] is [[irreflexive]]: <math>p \not\ll p</math> for all <math> p \in M </math>.

== Causal ==

* There are no closed causal (non-spacelike) curves.
* If both <math>p \prec q</math> and <math>q \prec p</math> then <math>p = q</math>

== Distinguishing ==

=== Past-distinguishing ===

* Two points <math>p, q \in M</math> which share the same chronological past are the same point:
:: <math>I^-(p) = I^-(q) \implies p = q </math>
* Equivalently, for any neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>p \in M</math> there exists a neighborhood <math>V \subset U, p \in V</math> such that no past-directed non-spacelike curve from <math>p</math> intersects <math>V</math> more than once.

=== Future-distinguishing ===

* Two points <math>p, q \in M</math> which share the same chronological future are the same point:
:: <math>I^+(p) = I^+(q) \implies p = q </math>
* Equivalently, for any neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>p \in M</math> there exists a neighborhood <math>V \subset U, p \in V</math> such that no future-directed non-spacelike curve from <math>p</math> intersects <math>V</math> more than once.

A [[spacetime]] is called '''distinguishing''' when it is both future and past distinguishing, that is, when each point is determined (distinguished) by its [[chronological future]] and also by its [[chronological past]].

== Strongly causal ==

* For every neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>p \in M</math> there exists a neighborhood <math>V \subset U, p \in V</math> through which no timelike curve passes more than once.
* For every neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>p \in M</math> there exists a neighborhood <math>V \subset U, p \in V</math> that is causally convex in <math>M</math> (and thus in <math>U</math>), that is, for each <math>q, q'</math> in <math>V</math> any causal curve in <math>M</math> from <math>q</math> to <math>q'</math> must be entirely contained in <math>U</math>.
* The [[Alexandrov topology]] (generated by the chronological futures and pasts of all the points) satisfies any of the following equivalent conditions: 
** (a) the Alexandrov topology is equal to the topology of the manifold.
** (b) the Alexandrov topology is Hausdorff.

== Stably causal ==

For each of the weaker causality conditions defined above, there are some manifolds satisfying the condition which can be made to violate it by arbitrarily small [[perturbation theory|perturbations]] of the metric. A spacetime <math>(M,g)</math> is called stably causal if it satisfies any of the following equivalent conditions:

# Causality is (<math>C^0</math>) stable: there exists a causal Lorentzian metric <math>g'</math> on <math>M</math> with the cones strictly wider than the original ones of <math>g</math> (that is, all the causal vectors for <math>g</math> are timelike vectors for <math>g'</math>).
# It admits a time function: there exists a continuous function <math>t</math> which is strictly increasing on causal (timelike or lightlike) curves.
# It admits a temporal function: there exists a [[Smoothness|smooth function]] <math>\tau</math> whose gradient <math>\nabla \tau</math> is timelike and past directed (in particular, <math>\tau</math> is then a time function).

Hawking (1969)<ref name="StablyCausal">S.W. Hawking, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2416157 ''The existence of cosmic time functions''] Proc. R. Soc. Lond. (1969), '''A308''', 433</ref> proved that condition 1 implies 2, and Bernal and Sánchez (2005)<ref>A. N. Bernal and M. Sánchez, ''Smoothness of time functions and the metric splitting of globally hyperbolic spacetimes'', Commun. Math. Phys. '''257''' (2005) 43-50.</ref> proved that 2 implies 3, while it is not difficult to check that condition 3 implies 1. See Sánchez<ref>M. Sánchez, ''Causal hierarchy of spacetimes, temporal functions and smoothness of Geroch's splitting. A revision.'' Matematica Contemporanea, Vol 29, 127-155 (2005). [https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0411143 arXiv:gr-qc/0411143] (Section 6).</ref> for a detailed account, as well as its relation with the folk problems of [[Geroch's splitting theorem#The "folk" problem|smoothability]]

== Causally continuous ==

A spacetime is called causally continuous when it satisfies: (a) it is distinguishing and (b) the chronological future <math>I^+(p)</math> and past <math>I^-(p)</math> varies continuously with the point <math>p</math>. 

There are several ways to express formally the meaning of this continuity. One of them starts by regarding <math>I^+</math> and <math>I^-</math> as set-valued functions from the manifold <math>M</math> into the set <math>\mathbb{P}(M)</math> of parts of <math>M</math> (i.e., the points of <math>\mathbb{P}(M)</math> are the subsets of <math>M</math>). Notice that <math>M</math> is endowed with a topology, and a topology on <math>\mathbb{P}(M)</math> can be defined as follows. For any compact <math>K \subset M</math>, the subsets of <math>M</math> not intersecting <math>K</math> form a subset of <math>\mathbb{P}(M)</math>, which is defined as open, then, these open sets are a base for the required topology. Thus, the condition (b) means that the maps <math>I^\pm: M \rightarrow \mathbb{P}(M)</math> are continuous as maps on topological spaces.<ref>E. Minguzzi and M. Sánchez, ''The causal hierarchy of spacetimes'' (2006). [https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0609119 arXiv:gr-qc/0609119] (Proposition 3.38 and Section 3.7).</ref>

== Causally simple ==
A spacetime is called causally simple when it satisfies: (a) it is causal and (b) <math>J^+(p)</math> and <math>J^-(p)</math> are closed for every point. 

Hawking and Ellis (1973), Beem, Ehrlich and Easley (1996)<ref>J. K. Beem, P. E. Ehrlich, and K. L. Easley, ''Global Lorentzian Geometry''. New York: Marcel Dekker Inc. (1996).</ref> and others traditionally required the condition of [[#Strongly causal|strong causality]]. However, following a result by Bernal and Sánchez (2007),<ref>A. N. Bernal and M. Sánchez, ''Globally hyperbolic spacetimes can be defined as "causal" instead of "strongly causal"'', Class. Quantum Grav. '''24''', 745-749 (2007).</ref> the simpler condition of causality is now used in the definition.

== Globally hyperbolic ==
{{Main|Globally hyperbolic manifold}}
* <math>\,M</math> is [[Causality conditions#causal|causal]] and every set <math>J^+(x) \cap J^-(y)</math> (for points <math>x,y \in M</math>) is [[Compact space|compact]].
[[Robert Geroch]] showed<ref name="GloballyHyperbolic">R. Geroch, [http://link.aip.org/link/?JMAPAQ/11/437/1 ''Domain of Dependence''] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20130224130421/http://link.aip.org/link/?JMAPAQ/11/437/1 |date=2013-02-24 }} J. Math. Phys. (1970) '''11''', 437–449</ref> that a spacetime is globally hyperbolic [[if and only if]] there exists a Cauchy surface for <math>M</math>. This means that:
* <math>M</math> is [[homeomorphism|topologically equivalent]] to <math>\mathbb{R} \times\!\, S</math> for some [[Cauchy surface]] <math>S.</math> (Here <math>\mathbb{R}</math> denotes the [[real line]]).

Moreover, it also admits the global orthogonal splitting obtained by Bernal and Sánchez (2005), thus showing that space and time can be globally distinguished (in a highly non-unique way).

== Properties of the hierarchy ==
It is worth pointing out that all the levels of the ladder are preserved when narrowing the cones (that is, when the original metric <math>g</math> is replaced by a metric <math>g'</math> whose causal vectors are included in the causal vectors for <math>g</math>), except causal continuity and causal simplicity, as shown by García-Parrado and Sánchez with an explicit counterexample.<ref>A. García-Parrado and M. Sánchez, ''Further properties of causal relationship: causal structure stability, new criteria for isocausality and counterexamples'', Class. Quantum Grav. '''22''' 4589-4619 (2005). [https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0507014 arXiv:math-ph/0507014].</ref>
